findings.title: Attacker-controlled 32-bit length prefix drives an unbounded heap allocation (up to ~2 GiB) before any payload is read
findings.impact: readBytes() sizes a Java array from a value it just read off the wire and allocates it before confirming that many bytes actually exist. Five bytes on the wire ('S' plus the length 0x7FFFFFFE) make the JVM attempt a ~2 GiB allocation. The failure mode is OutOfMemoryError, which is an Error rather than an IOException/MalformedFrameException, so it escapes the connection's protocol-error handling: the frame-reading thread dies and, because the heap pressure is process-wide, unrelated threads and co-tenants in the same JVM are collateral. The path is reachable by a malicious or MITM-ed broker before authentication (the Connection.Start server-properties field table contains longstr values and is parsed before credentials are sent), and post-authentication by any publisher able to set a longstr header or a byte-array ('x') field, so a minimally privileged publisher can knock over every Java consumer of a queue. Nothing in this class bounds the value; any bound has to come from a caller (frame max / max inbound body size), and the class is public API that callers can drive directly.
findings.evidence: final long contentLength = unsignedExtend(in.readInt()); if(contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE) { final byte [] buffer = new byte[(int)contentLength]; in.readFully(buffer); return buffer; }  -- reached from readLongstr() (field type 'S', line 163), from field type 'x' (line 211), and from the public readLongstr(). unsignedExtend() deliberately widens the int to the full 0..4294967295 range, and the only guard compares against Integer.MAX_VALUE, i.e. it accepts 2147483646.
findings.recommendation: Validate before allocating: reject any contentLength greater than the negotiated frame max, the configured maximum inbound body size, and the bytes actually remaining in the current frame, throwing MalformedFrameException. If genuinely large values must be supported, read incrementally into a growable buffer in bounded chunks rather than pre-allocating the declared size, so a lying length costs the attacker as much as it costs the victim.

findings.title: Unbounded recursion parsing nested field tables and arrays - StackOverflowError from a frame that fits inside the default frame max
findings.impact: readFieldValue -> readTable -> readFieldValue and readFieldValue -> readArray -> readFieldValue recurse once per nesting level with no depth counter anywhere in the class. Each level costs only 5 bytes on the wire for an array ('A' plus a 4-byte length) or 6 for a table (zero-length name, 'F', 4-byte length), so roughly 50 KB of input encodes ~10,000 levels and a payload comfortably inside the default 128 KiB frame max encodes over 25,000 - well past what a default JVM thread stack survives. Because the input fits inside the negotiated frame limit, the usual frame-size defence does not help. The resulting StackOverflowError is an Error, not MalformedFrameException, so it bypasses the clean protocol-error path and kills the frame-handling thread. The same input is also a memory amplifier: every table level allocates a HashMap plus a DataInputStream plus a TruncatedInputStream, roughly 30 bytes of heap per wire byte. Reachable pre-authentication through the Connection.Start server-properties table and post-authentication through message headers set by any publisher.
findings.evidence: case 'F': value = readTable(in); break;  (line 181) and  case 'A': value = readArray(in); break;  (line 184), with readTable calling readFieldValue(tableIn) at line 150 and readArray calling readFieldValue(arrayIn) at line 245. No depth argument, no counter, no limit on any of the three methods.
findings.recommendation: Thread a depth counter through readFieldValue/readTable/readArray and reject anything beyond a small maximum (real RabbitMQ tables are rarely deeper than 3-4 levels) with MalformedFrameException. Cap the total number of decoded elements per frame at the same time, and make sure the frame loop treats a parse failure as a protocol error that closes the connection rather than an unexpected crash.

findings.title: Table and array framing is driven by available() and silently accepts truncated input
findings.impact: Both loops terminate on available() == 0 and neither method verifies afterwards that exactly the declared tableLength / length bytes were consumed. Two consequences. (a) A frame that declares a table longer than the bytes actually present is not rejected - parsing simply stops and a partial table is handed to the application as if it were complete, while the broker, reading the same bytes, sees something else. That is a parser differential: identical wire bytes mean different things on the two sides, which is exactly the primitive used to smuggle or hide a header. (b) InputStream.available() is documented as an estimate, not a length. The constructor is public API that accepts any DataInputStream, so pointing this class at a socket-backed or otherwise not-fully-buffered stream makes available() return 0 for data that has not arrived yet, and every table and array decodes as EMPTY with no exception at all - headers disappear silently, which matters whenever headers carry routing, tenant or authorization data. The correctness of the whole scheme rests on TruncatedInputStream returning an exact remaining count, and that class is outside the audited scope, so it is an unverified assumption rather than a guarantee.
findings.evidence: while(tableIn.available() > 0) { String name = readShortstr(tableIn); Object value = readFieldValue(tableIn); if(!table.containsKey(name)) table.put(name, value); }  (readTable, lines 148-153) and  while(arrayIn.available() > 0) { Object value = readFieldValue(arrayIn); array.add(value); }  (readArray, lines 244-247). Neither is followed by a check that the TruncatedInputStream was drained exactly.
findings.recommendation: Track the remaining declared length explicitly with a counting wrapper instead of consulting available(), and after the loop assert the declared length was consumed exactly - throw MalformedFrameException on any shortfall or overrun. Either enforce or clearly document that the DataInputStream given to the public constructor must be fully buffered.

findings.title: Duplicate field-table keys are silently dropped first-wins, and short strings are decoded leniently - both enable header shadowing
findings.impact: The wire format allows a field name to appear more than once; this parser keeps the first occurrence and throws the rest away without an error. Other implementations - the broker itself, and clients in other languages - do not all resolve duplicates the same way, so the same frame can carry one value for the broker and a different value for a Java consumer. Wherever a header participates in a trust decision (an x-* attribute, a tenant or role tag, a value some upstream component validated and stamped), an attacker who can prepend a second copy of that key decides which value the Java side sees. Lenient UTF-8 decoding compounds it: new String(b, "utf-8") maps malformed byte sequences to U+FFFD instead of failing, so two distinct byte sequences on the wire can collapse into one Java String key and shadow each other. Neither behaviour is signalled to the caller.
findings.evidence: if(!table.containsKey(name)) table.put(name, value);  (lines 151-152) - later duplicates are discarded with no exception and no log. readShortstr (line 70) returns  new String(b, "utf-8")  which never throws on malformed input.
findings.recommendation: Treat a repeated field name as a malformed frame (MalformedFrameException) rather than resolving it silently; if compatibility forbids that, make the policy explicit and identical to the broker's. Decode short strings through a CharsetDecoder configured with CodingErrorAction.REPORT so invalid UTF-8 is a protocol error instead of a silently normalised key.

findings.title: Malformed-frame conditions surface as unchecked exceptions instead of MalformedFrameException
findings.impact: A length of 2 GiB or more raises UnsupportedOperationException, and the allocation just above it can raise OutOfMemoryError or, on other code paths, NegativeArraySizeException. None of these is an IOException or MalformedFrameException, so callers that catch protocol errors in order to close the connection cleanly do not catch them: a purely remote-triggered condition propagates out of the frame loop through an unexpected path, tears the connection down without the AMQP-level close, and is reported as if the client had a bug rather than as if the peer sent a bad frame. The guard itself is also weaker than it looks - comparing against Integer.MAX_VALUE admits a 2147483646-byte allocation, which is the case most worth refusing.
findings.evidence: } else { throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Very long byte vectors and strings not currently supported"); }  (lines 92-93), guarded by  if(contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE)  on line 87.
findings.recommendation: Throw MalformedFrameException (already imported and used in this class for the unrecognised-type case) for over-long lengths, and set the threshold at a configurable maximum far below Integer.MAX_VALUE. Ensure every failure this parser can produce from hostile input is a checked protocol exception the frame loop already handles.

findings.title: Silent 64-bit overflow converting AMQP timestamps to java.util.Date
findings.impact: The seconds value is fully attacker-controlled and is multiplied by 1000 with no range check, so the product wraps silently. An attacker can therefore pick a seconds value whose millisecond result is any value they want, including one in the past - the mapping is deterministic and trivial to invert. Applications that use the message timestamp for freshness, expiry, replay protection or ordering can be fed a message that looks recent when it is not, or ancient when it is not, without anything appearing malformed. Values near Long.MAX_VALUE produce a nonsensical Date instead of a rejected frame.
findings.recommendation: Use Math.multiplyExact, or check the value against Long.MAX_VALUE/1000 and a sane epoch window, and throw MalformedFrameException on anything out of range. Consider exposing an Instant rather than a Date so callers are not forced through a lossy conversion.

findings.title: No cap on table entries or array elements - small frames expand into large object graphs
findings.impact: Independently of the 2 GiB path in F-001 and the recursion in F-002, the decoder never counts what it has produced. Every element is a live object plus a slot in a growing ArrayList or HashMap, and the cheapest encodings amplify heavily: a one-byte 'V' element becomes an eight-byte reference in an ArrayList that over-allocates, a three-byte 's' element becomes a boxed Short outside the small-value cache, and a six-byte empty nested table becomes a HashMap plus two stream wrappers plus a parent map entry. A single frame at the default frame max therefore turns into several megabytes of live objects, per frame and per connection, all of it reachable by whoever can publish a message. That is not by itself fatal, but it removes any relationship between an attacker's bandwidth cost and the victim's memory cost.
findings.evidence: List<Object> array = new ArrayList<Object>(); while(arrayIn.available() > 0) { Object value = readFieldValue(arrayIn); array.add(value); }  (lines 243-247), and the equivalent unbounded HashMap growth in readTable (lines 145-153). Neither method counts entries or consults any configured limit.
findings.recommendation: Cap the number of entries per table, elements per array, and decoded objects per frame, rejecting the frame when a cap is exceeded. Where the sizes are known in advance, pre-size the collections instead of letting them double, and account decoded structures against the connection's memory budget.

findings.title: Mutability of the returned header map depends on remote input - empty tables come back immutable
findings.impact: A table with zero length returns Collections.emptyMap(), which is immutable; every other table returns a mutable HashMap. The type of object handed to application code is thus chosen by the remote peer. Ordinary consumer code that enriches or re-publishes a message - getHeaders().put(...) - works for every message that carries headers and throws UnsupportedOperationException for messages whose header table is empty. A publisher can trigger that in every consumer at will, at zero cost, simply by sending an empty table; whether the result is a nuisance, a poison message that is redelivered forever, or an outage depends entirely on the consumer's error handling.
findings.evidence: if (tableLength == 0) return Collections.emptyMap();  (line 143) versus  Map<String, Object> table = new HashMap<String, Object>();  (line 145).
findings.recommendation: Return the same map type from both branches - preferably an unmodifiable map in every case, so callers are forced to copy and behaviour never depends on remote input - and document the contract on the public readTable().

findings.title: Build generates source code by executing a script over inputs that live outside the repository and are not integrity-checked
findings.impact: The generate-sources phase runs a Groovy script that in turn executes codegen.py against a JSON specification taken from ${deps.dir}/rabbitmq_codegen, a path outside the module and overridable from the command line or by the in-umbrella profile, which silently redirects deps.dir to ${basedir}/.. when a file named UMBRELLA.md exists two levels up. The two largest generated classes in the shipped artifact (AMQP.java, AMQImpl.java) therefore come from content that is neither version-pinned nor checksum-verified here, and whoever controls that directory or that marker file controls code that ends up inside a signed, published jar. The build also has no dependency integrity gate (no enforcer rules, no checksum verification, no dependency locking), and some build/test-scope dependencies are on end-of-life lines - groovy-all 2.4.21 and jetty 9.4.58 - which no longer receive security fixes even though they run on developer and CI machines. Nothing here is exploitable by a remote peer at runtime; it is supply-chain surface.
findings.evidence: <script>${basedir}/codegen.py</script> with <spec>${codegen.dir}/amqp-rabbitmq-${codegen.spec_version}.json</spec> under the groovy-maven-plugin generate-amqp-sources execution (lines 613-636), <codegen.dir>${deps.dir}/rabbitmq_codegen</codegen.dir> (line 111), and the in-umbrella profile that rewrites deps.dir on the mere existence of ../../UMBRELLA.md (lines 133-141). Versions: <groovy.all.version>2.4.21</groovy.all.version> (line 81), <jetty.version>9.4.58.v20250814</jetty.version> (line 70).
findings.recommendation: Pin the codegen specification to a checked-in, checksum-verified copy (or a git submodule at a fixed commit) and fail the build when the file's digest does not match. Add maven-enforcer rules plus dependency checksum verification so plugin and dependency resolution cannot be silently substituted, and move the end-of-life build/test dependencies onto supported lines.
